items.passage: Scroll through any social media feed and you'll find someone extolling the virtues of a 5 am start, a cold shower and a meticulously colour-coded diary. The message, implicit or otherwise, is that time not spent improving oneself is time wasted. It's an appealing idea, not least because it suggests that success lies entirely within our control. It also flatters those who already have the time and money to follow such regimes. Yet the more I read about these routines, the more I suspect they say less about productivity than about anxiety. A walk without a podcast, an afternoon with nothing scheduled — these are increasingly framed as indulgences to be earned rather than as ordinary parts of a life. Research over the past thirty years has overturned that view. During deep sleep, the brain appears to replay the day's experiences, strengthening some connections while allowing others to fade. This may explain why students who sleep after learning tend to remember more than those who stay up revising, even when the latter spend longer with their books. While we recognise the venue's contribution to the town's cultural life — indeed, many of our members are regular patrons — and appreciate that it employs a number of local people, we have serious reservations about permitting events to continue until 2 am on weekdays. Noise from departing customers is already a recurring problem after midnight, and residents with young children or early starts have been disproportionately affected. Several have also reported litter and broken glass on the riverside path. We would therefore urge the council to consider a compromise: a later licence at weekends only, coupled with a commitment from the venue to place staff at the exits to encourage quiet departures. We would welcome the opportunity to discuss this further, and have invited the venue's management to our next meeting on 4 May.
Yours sincerely,
Jordan Ellis, Chair

items.passage: Does listening to an audiobook count as reading? The question provokes surprisingly strong feelings. Sales of audiobooks have grown steadily for over a decade, so the debate is unlikely to go away. Purists insist that something is lost when the words reach us through another person's voice: the listener no longer controls the pace, cannot easily linger over a sentence, and is at the mercy of the narrator's interpretation. Enthusiasts reply that stories were told aloud long before they were written down, and that a skilled narrator can illuminate a text rather than distort it. Research, for what it's worth, suggests that comprehension of straightforward narrative is broadly similar whether a text is heard or read, though the picture changes with dense, technical material, where the ability to reread seems to matter. Perhaps the more useful question is not whether listening counts, but what we want from a particular book — and whether, for some of us, the real choice is between an audiobook and no book at all.
